HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e114.summary: Title rubric for the first question of the Prologue: whether God is the subject of sacred Scripture under an abyssal or absolute aspect (ratio).

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e123.summary: States the question: whether God is subject in sacred theology under an abyssal or absolute aspect, i.e., whether theology considers God under the infinite ratio of deity itself or under some restricted ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e130.summary: First principal argument that God is subject under the absolute ratio: no science considers its subject under a ratio intrinsically repugnant to it, and a finite ratio is intrinsically repugnant to God, who is formally infinite.
claims: No science treats its subject under a ratio intrinsically repugnant to that subject.
A finite ratio is intrinsically repugnant to God, who is formally and intrinsically infinite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e144.summary: Second principal argument: as a thing stands to being so it stands to being known (Metaph. 2), whence modes of understanding follow modes of being; since God's being is infinite, he must be known under an infinite ratio. Then gives the argument to the contrary (sed contra): if God were subject under an infinite ratio, theology would be an infinite science, since habits are specified by their objects.
claims: Modes of understanding follow modes of being, so infinite being should be understood under an infinite ratio.
Contra: since habits are specified by their objects, a theology whose subject is God under an infinite ratio would itself be infinite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e168.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the outcome of the question: God is the subject of theology under a special ratio, as the supremely lovable truth proportioned to the rational soul not yet perfected by the habit of the light of glory.
claims: God is the subject of theology under a special ratio: as the supremely lovable truth proportioned to the rational soul not yet perfected by the light of glory.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e181.summary: Methodological preface stating that this question, and most questions of the whole work, will follow a fixed order of procedure once the terms are presupposed or explained.
claims: The work follows a standard order of procedure in its questions.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e194.summary: First step of the method: Thomas will state his conclusion first, since it is the target to which all supporting and contrary reasons are related; like archers with a mark (Aristotle, Ethics 1), fixing the mind's eye on the conclusion makes it easier to grasp what supports and what opposes it.
claims: The conclusion should be stated first because it functions as the target by reference to which all arguments are evaluated.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e223.summary: Second step of the method: Thomas will bring in contrary opinions with their motives and show that their reasons do not conclude.
claims: Contrary opinions will be presented with their reasons and shown to be inconclusive.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e232.summary: Third step of the method: Thomas will then confirm his conclusion as best he can; this order is justified by Boethius's maxim that vices must be uprooted before virtues are planted — sophistical reasons (the 'thorns' troubling the truth) are removed before true reasons are introduced.
claims: Refutation of false reasons should precede confirmation of the true conclusion.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e261.summary: Fourth step of the method: Thomas will reply to the principal arguments with which the question was opened.
claims: The principal arguments will be answered last.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e268.summary: States Thomas's conclusion: God is the subject of sacred Scripture under a special ratio, not under the absolute or abyssal ratio. Although we lack names adequate to express it, the subject can be described as 'the supremely lovable true, as proportioned to the rational soul not yet perfected by the habit of the light of glory.' 'True' serves as the genus common to all sciences, while 'lovable' differentiates theology from both practical and speculative sciences.
claims: God is subject of theology under a special, not an absolute or abyssal, ratio.
The subject of theology may be described as the supremely lovable truth proportioned to the wayfaring rational soul.
'Truth' is the generic element common to all sciences' subjects; 'lovable' distinguishes theology from both speculative and practical sciences.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e299.summary: Explains the description of theology's subject: a subject's ratio should be named in relation to the end — truth for speculative sciences, the operable for practical sciences — and since the love of God is the end of theology, its object is properly 'the lovable true.' 'Proportioned' distinguishes our theology from God's own science, which grasps the subject under the infinite ratio; 'not yet perfected' distinguishes it from the theology of the blessed, who are perfected by the light of glory.
claims: A subject's formal ratio should be expressed in relation to the end of the science.
Since the love of God is theology's end, its object is properly the lovable true.
Our theology differs from God's science by being proportioned to our intellect, and from the knowledge of the blessed by being had without the light of glory.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e337.summary: Lists opponents of this account: those who hold theology to be speculative, those who hold it practical, those who hold it both (all deferred to q.4 a.4), and especially those who hold that God is subject of both the divine science and ours under the same ratio, namely the absolute ratio of deity. Since all agree God knows himself under that absolute ratio, these thinkers argue in many ways that our theology too considers God under it.
claims: Some hold that God is the subject of both divine and human theology under the same absolute ratio of deity.
The questions of whether theology is speculative or practical are deferred to q.4 a.4.
concepts: theologia in se vs theologia nostra

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e373.summary: First two arguments of the opponents: (1) a subject is considered under that ratio under which all things in the science are considered, and everything in Scripture is either God or attributed to God; (2) the subject of a science and of its principles is the same under the same ratio, and God is subject of the articles of faith (the principles of theology) under the absolute ratio.
claims: Since everything in theology is God or related to God, God is subject under the absolute ratio.
Since God is the subject of the articles of faith under the absolute ratio, and a science and its principles share the same subject and ratio, theology too treats God under the absolute ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e395.summary: Third argument of the opponents: the subject's ratio must contain fundamentally and virtually all the truths contained in the habit, which no special or contracted ratio can do in theology.
claims: The ratio of the subject must virtually contain all the truths of the science, which only the absolute ratio of deity can do in theology.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e409.summary: Fourth argument of the opponents: the absolute ratio of deity is prior to every contracted ratio, so if our theology considered God under a contracted ratio there would have to be a prior science considering him under the absolute ratio.
claims: If theology treated God under a contracted ratio, a prior science treating him under the absolute ratio would be required.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e425.summary: Fifth argument of the opponents: in the theology of the blessed God is subject under the absolute ratio, so also in ours (supported by Ps 47:9, 'As we have heard, so have we seen'). The antecedent is proved three ways: otherwise the desire of the blessed would remain unfulfilled; their intuitive knowledge terminates at the divine essence in its own existence, not under a contracted ratio; and Augustine says our full joy is to enjoy the Trinity.
claims: The blessed know God under the absolute ratio, and our theology should correspond to theirs.
Otherwise the desire of the blessed would be unfulfilled.
Intuitive cognition terminates at the divine essence itself, not at a contracted ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e466.summary: Sixth argument of the opponents: the noblest science must consider its subject under the noblest ratio, and the absolute ratio of deity is nobler than any special or contracted one.
claims: The noblest science should treat its subject under the noblest ratio, which is the absolute ratio of deity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e479.summary: Seventh argument of the opponents: the objective ratio belongs either to God's side, in which case it is absolute and infinite, or to our intellect's side, in which case it could not distinguish theology from other sciences, since all agree in being received in the same intellect.
claims: An objective ratio on God's side would be absolute and infinite; one on the intellect's side could not distinguish sciences.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e492.summary: Eighth argument of the opponents: a thing is subject in a science under the ratio by which it is first presented to the intellect in that science, and that is the absolute ratio of deity.
claims: The subject's ratio is what first meets the intellect in a science, and in theology that is the absolute ratio of deity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e503.summary: Raises the objection to the opponents: if the absolute ratio of deity is intrinsically and formally infinite, our theology, being specified by its object, would be infinite.
claims: If theology's subject is the formally infinite ratio of deity, theology would be infinite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e515.summary: First line of reply by some opponents: infinity is not part of God's formal ratio but a property (passio) that, by our mode of understanding, follows upon deity and is attributed to God as an attribute; a property, whether really or conceptually distinct, is posterior to and not included in the subject's formal ratio.
claims: Infinity is not of the formal ratio of God but a property consequent on deity in our mode of understanding.
A property is not included in the formal ratio of its subject.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e535.summary: Second supporting argument for the opponents' reply: whatever belongs to a thing's formal ratio is apprehended when the thing is apprehended; but God's existence is quasi self-evident, while many philosophers doubted his infinity.
claims: Whatever belongs to a thing's formal ratio is apprehended with it.
Philosophers knew God yet doubted his infinity, so infinity is not of his formal ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e548.summary: Third supporting argument: the blessed see deity but do not see God's infinity.
claims: The blessed see the deity without seeing its infinity, so infinity is not of the formal ratio of deity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e557.summary: Fourth supporting argument: a privative ratio is not formally included in a positive one; infinity is privative, deity positive.
claims: Infinity is a privative ratio and so cannot be formally included in the positive ratio of deity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e568.summary: Thomas rejects the claim that infinity is not of God's formal ratio. What is pure act and founds infinite perfections is essentially infinite: if infinite perfection did not belong to it essentially, it would found them as a receptive potency and could not be pure act. That deity is such is known to every Christian and is also affirmed by Aristotle (Metaph. 5, on the perfect being) with Averroes's commentary identifying that being as God.
claims: What is pure act and founds infinite perfections is essentially infinite.
If infinite perfection belonged to it non-essentially, it would found perfections as a receptive potency and so would not be pure act.
Infinity is therefore of the formal and intrinsic ratio of deity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e624.summary: Second argument that infinity belongs to deity's formal ratio: just as that is formally white which makes everything joined to it really white, so that is formally infinite which makes everything identical with it really infinite. God's wisdom is really infinite not qua wisdom (otherwise all wisdom would be infinite) but by identity with deity; so deity formally includes infinity. The argument is given in two redactions.
claims: What makes everything identical with it really infinite is itself formally infinite.
Divine wisdom is infinite by its identity with deity, not as wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e656.summary: Third argument: if infinity were not of deity's formal ratio, there would be a nobler ratio than deity, since a ratio formally expressing infinite perfection is nobler than one that does not; but this is false both theologically and philosophically, since Aristotle (Metaph. 12) calls God noble at the summit of all nobility.
claims: If infinity were not of the formal ratio of deity, some ratio would be nobler than deity, which is false.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e680.summary: Fourth argument: what is an infinite sea of substance includes infinity in its formal and substantial ratio, and according to John Damascene God is such an infinite sea of substance.
claims: God, as an infinite sea of substance, includes infinity in his formal ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e693.summary: Fifth argument (numbered 3 in the text): that than which nothing greater can be thought in magnitude of perfection includes infinity of perfection in its formal ratio, since what includes such infinity is thought greater than what does not; Anselm affirms God is such.
claims: That than which no greater can be thought must formally include infinity of perfection.
God is that than which no greater can be thought.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e713.summary: Sixth argument (numbered 4): just as being formally finite belongs to the ratio of every created power, so being formally infinite belongs to the ratio of the divine quiddity; creature is to finite, limited being as creator is to infinite, unlimited being.
claims: As formal finitude belongs to the ratio of every creature, formal infinity belongs to the ratio of the divine quiddity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e726.summary: Reply to the first argument of the opponents' reply: Thomas denies that infinity is a property; it is rather like a substantial difference, so that if deity could be completely defined (as if God had genus and difference), infinity would be posited as the difference. Hence infinity is predicated of deity in the first mode of per se predication, not the second.
claims: Infinity is not a property of deity but functions like a substantial difference.
Infinity is predicated of deity in the first mode of per se predication.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e746.summary: Reply to the second argument: whatever is of a thing's formal ratio is apprehended with it only if the thing is apprehended perfectly, and no philosopher apprehended God perfectly.
claims: Apprehension of a thing includes everything in its formal ratio only if the apprehension is perfect.
No philosopher apprehended God perfectly.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e758.summary: Reply to the third argument: the blessed see both deity and its infinity, but not infinitely or in an infinite mode, and hence not under the ratio of the infinite.
claims: The blessed see God's infinity but not infinitely, and so not under the ratio of the infinite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e769.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: 'infinite' is privative only in the imposition of the name, not in what the thing is; in reality it is something most real and maximally positive.
claims: Infinity is privative only in name; in reality it is maximally positive.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e782.summary: A second response by others to the objection that our theology would be infinite: a science of the infinite is infinite only when it attains not only the infinite thing but also the ratio of infinity, as God's science does; our theology attains the infinite thing and the ratio of deity, but infinity is merely annexed to the object, not itself objected.
claims: A science is infinite only if it attains the ratio of infinity, not merely an infinite thing.
In our theology deity is objected but infinity is only annexed to the object.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e806.summary: Thomas rejects that response on three counts: it assumes falsely that infinity is annexed rather than intrinsic to deity; it contradicts the opponents' own position that God is subject under the same ratio in God's science and ours, since a ratio directly including infinity and one including it only by annexation are not the same; and it in fact supports Thomas's view, since it implies the object is restricted by some special ratio as presented to us.
claims: Infinity is intrinsic to deity, not annexed to it.
The response is self-contradictory given the claim of a single ratio in divine and human theology.
The response effectively concedes that God is objected to us under a special, restricted ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e837.summary: A third response by others denies the consequence that a science of the infinite is infinite, citing natural philosophy (Physics 3), which treats the infinite without being infinite.
claims: A science about the infinite need not be infinite, as physics treats the infinite without being infinite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e846.summary: Second argument of this third response: a science takes its species from its object without being of the same species as it; likewise it may take quantity from its object without being of the same quantity — a science of stone is not stony, so a science of the infinite need not be infinite.
claims: A science derives its species from its object without sharing the object's nature, so it need not share the object's infinity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e863.summary: Third argument of this response: if a finite act could not attain an infinite object, no creature could be beatified, yet Augustine says our heart is restless until it rests in God.
claims: A finite act can attain an infinite object, otherwise no creature could be beatified.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e881.summary: Fourth argument of this response: our intellect has far greater scope in knowing than in being; it knows all things but is not all things.
claims: The intellect's cognitive scope exceeds its being, so a finite intellect can know the infinite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e892.summary: Fifth argument of this response: as power stands to effect, so subject stands to science, and an infinite power can cause a finite effect. These thinkers therefore hold that a science takes its species from its object but its quantitative mode from the receiving subject; received in a finite subject it is finite even if about an infinite object, as the different seeing of eagle and owl comes from the eye, not the object.
claims: Science takes its species from its object but its quantity from its receiving subject.
A science received in a finite subject is finite even if about an infinite object.
concepts: species vs quantity of a habit

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e927.summary: Objection put to the holders of the third response: a science is equated to its proper object, so how can a finite science be equal to an infinite object?
claims: A science must be adequate to its proper object, which seems impossible for a finite science of an infinite object.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e936.summary: Their reply: although the finite cannot equal the infinite in the same genus of adequation, it can in another genus. Just as an indivisible intelligible species can equal a divisible line in representational rather than quantitative being, so a finite act or habit can equal the infinite God not in natural being but in expressive or cognized being.
claims: The finite can equal the infinite in a different genus of adequation.
A finite habit can equal God in representational (cognized) being though not in natural being.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e962.summary: Thomas rejects this: between a proper measure and the measured there must be adequation, neither exceeding the other; the subject taken under its subjectal ratio is the proper measure of a science; hence whatever is comprehended in the subject under that ratio could be known by the science, so that one with theology would know infinite things if God were subject under the infinite ratio.
claims: There must be adequation between a proper measure and what it measures.
The subject under its subjectal ratio is the proper measure of the science.
If God were subject under the infinite ratio, the theologian would know infinite things.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e989.summary: Reply to the first argument of the third response (physics treats the infinite): the cases differ, since Physics 3 treats potential infinity and the meaning of the name, and Physics 8 treats God's infinity not under the infinite ratio but by comparison with a determinate effect, motion, and only as to the fact that it is, not what it is.
claims: Physics treats potential infinity and God's infinity only relatively, through motion, not under the ratio of the infinite.
Physics knows of God's infinity only quia est, not quid est.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1015.summary: Continuation of the preceding reply: the allegation helps the opponents little, since Aristotle himself says the infinite as infinite, i.e., under the ratio of infinity, is unknown.
claims: The infinite under the ratio of infinity is unknown, as Aristotle says.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1026.summary: Reply to the second argument: just as a power is commensurate with its adequate object, so a science is necessarily commensurate with its subject taken under its formal ratio, and such virtual commensuration requires equality. Moreover, the inference 'not adequate in specific being, therefore not adequate in quantitative being' moves fallaciously from the unqualified to the qualified destructively.
claims: A science is necessarily commensurate with its subject under its formal ratio.
Arguing from lack of specific equality to lack of quantitative equality commits the fallacy a simpliciter ad secundum quid.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1061.summary: Reply to the third argument (beatitude): the creature is beatified by an infinite object but not under the ratio of infinity; it suffices for beatitude to see a good that cannot be referred to a greater good, in which the will rests delighted for its own sake.
claims: The blessed are beatified by an infinite object but not under the ratio of infinity.
Beatitude requires seeing a good not referable to a greater good, in which the will rests.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1074.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: although the intellect is not all the things it knows, it is commensurate with its adequate object, which comprehends whatever it can know.
claims: The intellect is commensurate with its adequate object, which includes everything it can know.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1087.summary: Reply to the fifth argument (infinite power producing finite effects). One might say the cases differ because God's power acts freely through will, while an object moves naturally; Thomas declines this, since he will argue at the end of Book 4 that the beatific object moves the blessed freely, as a voluntary mirror. Instead, conceding the major, he says God's infinite power produces externally only finite things, being determined by finite ideal rationes; under the infinite ratio it produces only the Son and Holy Spirit. Against the claim that science takes its quantity from its receiving subject, he argues that even a theology created without a subject would be finite, since every creature is finite; the eagle/owl analogy fails because their visions do not differ in species, while finite and infinite science differ more than generically (one is a creature, the other the creator). He concludes that the opponents' arguments for the absolute ratio do not conclude.
claims: God's infinite power produces externally only finite effects, determined by finite ideal rationes.
Under the infinite ratio God's power produces only the Son and the Holy Spirit.
A created science is finite as a creature regardless of the subject receiving it.
Finite and infinite science differ more than generically, so the eagle/owl analogy fails.
The beatific object moves the blessed freely, as a voluntary mirror (to be argued in Book 4).

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1173.summary: Reply to the opponents' first argument for the absolute ratio: granted that everything in theology is God or attributed to God, this shows only that God is theology's subject, not that he is subject under the infinite or absolute ratio. A second version follows.
claims: The attribution of all theological matter to God proves only that God is subject, not under which ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1191.summary: Alternative reply to the first argument: the argument is defective because the minor is not subsumed under the major; if it were, it would be false, since not everything in theology is considered under the absolute ratio of deity, which is simply incomprehensible.
claims: Not everything in theology is considered under the absolute ratio of deity, which is incomprehensible.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1207.summary: Reply to the second argument (principles of faith): Thomas denies the major. The habit of the articles of faith is faith, which differs in species from the habit of theology; though they can have the same subject, it must be under different rationes, since habits differing in species cannot have the same object under the same ratio. That faith and theology differ in species is shown by their coexistence in one subject, since accidents differing only numerically cannot coexist in the same subject. The minor is also false, since God is not subject in the articles under the infinite ratio.
claims: The habit of the articles of faith is faith, which differs in species from the habit of theology.
Habits differing in species cannot have the same object under the same ratio.
Faith and theology coexist in one subject and therefore differ in species.
God is not subject of the articles of faith under the infinite ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1242.summary: Reply to the third argument (virtual containment): the formal ratio of a subject need not contain all things in the science as prior to them in entity or dignity; in medicine the formal ratio is 'curable', yet human substance, nobler than the curable as such, is treated there. It suffices that the subject's ratio contains them according to the science's mode of knowing.
claims: The subject's ratio need only contain the science's contents according to that science's mode of knowing, not as prior in entity or dignity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1266.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: there is indeed a prior and nobler science than our theology, but it is the science of the creator, not of any creature.
claims: The science prior to our theology, which treats God under the absolute ratio, is God's own science.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1277.summary: Reply to the fifth argument (theology of the blessed): Thomas concedes the consequence but denies the antecedent. The blessed enjoy an infinite good and thereby have every desire filled, though they do not see it infinitely and so not under the infinite ratio. Inferring 'they see intuitively, therefore under the infinite ratio' commits the fallacy of the consequent; the Augustine citation is answered the same way.
claims: The blessed do not know God under the infinite ratio, though they enjoy an infinite good.
Intuitive vision does not entail vision under the infinite ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1303.summary: Reply to the sixth argument (noblest science): following Priscian, a superlative can mean what surpasses all others, or simply the positive with 'very.' In the first sense the minor is false, since only God's science is noblest and only it has the absolute, infinite ratio of the subject; in the second sense the syllogism is granted but concludes only that our theology considers its subject under a very noble ratio, which can be finite, contracted and special.
claims: Only God's science is noblest in the strict superlative sense.
Our theology is noblest only in the sense of 'very noble', which is compatible with a finite, special ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1349.summary: Reply to the seventh argument: the objective ratio belongs fundamentally to God's side, since an object measures act and habit by its formal ratio; but because what is measured is finite, the ratio by which the object measures the habit or act must be finite.
claims: The objective ratio is founded on God's side.
Because the measured act or habit is finite, the ratio by which God measures it must be finite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1371.summary: Anticipates two difficulties arising from the reply to the seventh argument: (1) if the special ratio is a precision or restriction of God from his absolute, infinite ratio, either there is an intrinsic precision in God or the special ratio is not on God's side; (2) since such precision is made only by our act of understanding, the ratio of the object would be caused by the act rather than preceding it, the reverse of the true order.
claims: The special ratio seems either to posit something intrinsic in God or not to be on God's side.
The special ratio seems to be caused by the act of understanding, inverting the order of object and act.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1397.summary: Reply to the first difficulty: the precision posits nothing intrinsic in God, since limitation would imply imperfection; it belongs to him extrinsically insofar as he is the measure of something finite and limited. Yet it is still on God's side, since a measure belongs to the measuring thing — as when the soul divides and numbers the first motion, the numbering belongs to the motion and not to the soul, otherwise time would be a property of the soul rather than of motion (Physics 4).
claims: The special ratio posits nothing intrinsic in God but belongs to him extrinsically as measure of something finite.
A measure belongs to the side of the measuring thing even when the measuring is effected by the soul, as time belongs to motion.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1437.summary: One possible reply to the second difficulty, given by some doctors: the object under its objective ratio contributes to the act and habit as terminating them, since it is their measure, but not as moving and causing them, since in that respect they come about by creation under an ideal (also special) ratio. So it is not unfitting that the precision, aptitudinally pre-existing in the object, be completed by the very act it terminates, since a terminus presupposes what it terminates.
claims: The object terminates act and habit as their measure but does not cause them, which is done by creation under an ideal ratio.
The precision can be completed by the act it terminates, since a terminus presupposes what it terminates.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1470.summary: Objection to the previous reply: it is impossible for an act to be caused under one ratio and terminated under another.
claims: An act cannot be caused under one ratio and terminated under another.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1478.summary: Reply: there is no impossibility; if God created an act of hearing in the ear, it would still terminate at sound, not at the ideal ratio under which it was created.
claims: An act created by God under an ideal ratio still terminates at its proper object, as created hearing terminates at sound.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1491.summary: Thomas does not rest on that solution: it holds for theology as possessed by prophets and apostles, who received it by infusion of the Holy Spirit (2 Pet 1:21), but not for theology as we acquire it by study and teaching, which is not created in us under an ideal ratio. Hence he holds it not unfitting that the objective ratio, as to its formal completion, follow and in some way depend upon the act of intellect, while as to its fundamental being it precedes the act and in no way depends on it.
claims: Infused theology (of prophets and apostles) differs from acquired theology (ours) in its mode of acquisition.
Our theology is acquired by study, not created under an ideal ratio.
The objective ratio precedes the act fundamentally but depends on the act for its formal completion.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1536.summary: Reply to the eighth argument: the major is not true, since those possessing a science often disagree about its objective ratio, as with the subject of metaphysics; if the objective ratio occurred first, such disputes would not exist. The minor is also false, since the infinite absolute ratio of deity cannot first occur to a finite intellect.
claims: The objective ratio of a science is not necessarily what first occurs to the intellect, as disputes about the subject of metaphysics show.
The infinite ratio of deity cannot first occur to a finite intellect.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1556.summary: Transitional sentence: having uprooted the thorns that trouble the truth, Thomas will now confirm his position.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1565.summary: First confirmation: if God were subject of our theology under the absolute ratio of deity, God's science and ours would be of the same species, since habits are specified by their objects under their subjectal rationes and God knows himself under the absolute ratio; but this consequent is impossible.
claims: If our theology shared God's absolute ratio of its subject, it would be of the same species as God's science, which is impossible.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1589.summary: Second confirmation: in things essentially ordered as exceeding and exceeded, what is adequate to the exceeding habit is never adequate to the exceeded; God's science and ours are so ordered; since a subject under its subjectal ratio is adequate to its science, nothing can be subject under the same ratio in both.
claims: What is adequate to an exceeding habit cannot be adequate to an exceeded one.
God's science and ours are related as exceeding and exceeded, so they cannot share the same subject under the same ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1608.summary: Third confirmation: if theology's subject were God under the abyssal, infinite ratio, through theology we would know infinite things, which every theologian experiences to be false. The consequence holds because the subject under its subjectal ratio stands to the science as the adequate object stands to a power: nothing is contained under the object that the power cannot reach. Since infinite things are contained and represented in God under the ratio of deity, theology would know them. Hence God must be subject under a special ratio.
claims: If God were subject under the infinite ratio, theologians would know infinite things, which experience shows false.
The subject of a science stands to it as the adequate object stands to a power.
Therefore God must be subject in our theology under a special ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1650.summary: Thomas states that his position does not depart from 'our venerable doctor, Brother Giles' (Giles of Rome), who expressed the same truth in other words: Giles's 'special ratio' means only a restriction of the abyssal ratio in the object, and his use of the name 'glorifier' (glorificator) is not essential, since Giles admits no apt name exists; it signals that the ratio must be named by reference to theology's end, the glory of eternal life consisting principally in the love of God. Those who argue against the term 'glorificator' therefore attack the word rather than Giles's intention, though Thomas will answer them out of respect for him.
claims: Thomas's account of theology's subject agrees in substance with Giles of Rome's.
Giles's 'special ratio' means a restriction of the abyssal ratio in the object.
The term 'glorificator' names the subject in relation to theology's end, eternal glory consisting principally in the love of God.
Critics of 'glorificator' attack the name rather than Giles's intention.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1715.summary: First argument against Giles's term 'glorificator': if God is subject as glorifier, the reduplication refers either to the divine glorifying power (then it is the same as the infinite ratio, since that power is the divine essence), or to a created effect in the glorified (then theology's formal object would be something created), or to God's act of glorifying (which collapses into one of the first two, depending on whether the act is on God's side or the glorified's).
claims: If 'glorifier' means divine power, it is identical with the infinite essence.
If it means the created effect, theology's formal object would be created.
If it means the act of glorifying, it reduces to one of the other two options.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1741.summary: Second argument against 'glorificator': what is investigated in a science cannot be its objective ratio, since the subject and its formal ratio are presupposed, not inquired into; but the ratio of glorifier is investigated in theology, being posterior to the rationes of goodness and wisdom, which are themselves investigated.
claims: A science presupposes rather than investigates its subject's formal ratio.
The ratio of glorifier is investigated in theology, so it cannot be its formal ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1763.summary: Third argument against 'glorificator': it signifies either the divine nature alone in Christ, the human alone, or both. Not the human alone, otherwise Scripture would not treat the Father and Holy Spirit per se, who did not assume human nature; not both, for the same reason; therefore only the divine nature.
claims: 'Glorifier' cannot signify Christ's human nature alone or both natures, since then Scripture would not treat the Father and Spirit per se.
Therefore it signifies only the divine nature.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1782.summary: Fourth argument against 'glorificator': the formal ratio of a subject is that into which everything in the science is ultimately resolved, but many rationes belonging to God — deity, Trinity, wisdom, goodness — are prior to that of glorifier.
claims: The subject's formal ratio is that into which all the science's contents are ultimately resolved.
Deity, Trinity, wisdom and goodness are prior to the ratio of glorifier.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1798.summary: Fifth argument against 'glorificator': the ratio of glorifier is infinite, since otherwise it could not satisfy the blessed; so the position falls into what it sought to avoid.
claims: The ratio of glorifier must be infinite to satisfy the blessed, so it does not avoid the infinite ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1809.summary: Sixth argument against 'glorificator': the same thing under the same ratio should not be the subject of an entire science and of each of its parts; but God is subject under a special ratio in the particular books of the canon, so not in the whole of Scripture.
claims: The subject of the whole of Scripture cannot be under the same special ratio as the subject of its individual books.
concepts: subject of a whole science vs its parts

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1822.summary: Seventh argument against 'glorificator', by another opponent: 'glorifier' means either that by which God formally glorifies, which is deity itself (so the subject would be under the ratio of deity), or the relation of the glorifier to the glorified, by which God is called glorifier as he is called creator from creation existing in the creature; then an extrinsic denomination would be the formal ratio of the science's subject.
claims: 'Glorifier' reduces either to deity itself or to an extrinsic denomination, neither of which serves as a special formal ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1844.summary: Eighth argument against 'glorificator': God is not subject under a ratio by which the truths determined in the science do not belong to him; truths like the Trinity do not belong to God as glorifier, since God was triune from eternity before glorifying; properties belong to the subject through the subject's ratio, but God is not triune insofar as he glorifies.
claims: Truths determined in theology, like the Trinity, do not belong to God by virtue of his being glorifier.
God was triune from eternity before glorifying anyone.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1866.summary: General reply to the arguments against 'glorificator': since theology is given by God as an instrument directing us to eternal happiness, its objective ratio is best expressed in relation to that end, and 'glorifier' is such a name.
claims: Theology is a God-given instrument directing us to eternal happiness.
Its objective ratio is therefore best named in relation to that end, as 'glorifier' does.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1883.summary: Reply to the first argument against 'glorificator': the term reduplicates the divine power, which is the divine essence, but taken commensurately, according to its proportion to our intellect.
claims: 'Glorifier' signifies the divine power taken as proportioned to our intellect.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1894.summary: Reply to the second argument: as in other sciences the subject's ratio is presupposed as to complete knowledge, so in theology the ratio of glorifier is presupposed by faith (Heb 11:6, that God rewards those who seek him), though it is still investigated as to perfect knowledge.
claims: The ratio of glorifier is presupposed by faith but investigated in theology for perfect knowledge.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1912.summary: Reply to the third argument: 'glorifier' signifies the divine nature, but with the restriction mentioned earlier.
claims: 'Glorifier' signifies the divine nature under the special restriction.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1921.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: a ratio can be prior to others such that they resolve into it either simply or with respect to us. Taken simply, the major is false; taken with respect to us, the minor is false: though glorifier is not simply prior, it is prior in relation to the theologian, who considers everything in theology in relation to his beatitude.
claims: Resolution of a science's contents into its subject's ratio may be simply or quoad nos.
The ratio of glorifier is prior quoad nos, since the theologian considers everything in relation to beatitude.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1947.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: the ratio of glorifier is infinite materially, by reason of its substrate, the divine essence, but not formally.
claims: The ratio of glorifier is materially infinite but formally finite.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1958.summary: Reply to the sixth argument: God is subject under a special ratio both in the whole of Scripture and in each particular book, but not with the same degree of specialness; the ratio is more contracted with respect to a given book and less with respect to the whole.
claims: Theology's subject is under a special ratio in both the whole of Scripture and its parts, but with varying degrees of contraction.
concepts: subject of a whole science vs its parts

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1979.summary: Reply to the seventh argument: answered as in the immediately preceding replies to the first and third arguments.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1988.summary: Reply to the eighth argument and its confirmation: answered as earlier in the reply to the third argument brought against the principal conclusion.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e1999.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: although a finite ratio is intrinsically repugnant to God in being, it is not extrinsically repugnant in being considered. Just as an intrinsically finite thing can relate to an infinite termination extrinsically — the center point of a sphere, finite in itself, can terminate infinite lines — so an intrinsically infinite thing can relate to an extrinsic finite termination.
claims: A finite ratio is repugnant to God intrinsically in being but not extrinsically in consideration.
Something intrinsically infinite can stand under a finite extrinsic termination, as a finite point terminates infinitely many lines.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e2028.summary: Reply to the second principal argument: for the Metaph. 2 principle it suffices that what is understood truly be in reality; the mode of being need not always correspond uniformly to the mode of understanding, otherwise quiddities understood separately would exist separately — Plato's error. As the mathematician conceives non-qualitatively what is truly qualified, the theologian conceives finitely what is truly infinite.
claims: The mode of understanding need not correspond uniformly to the mode of being.
Requiring such correspondence leads to Plato's error of separate quiddities.
The theologian may conceive the infinite finitely, as the mathematician abstracts quantity from quality.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e2057.summary: Objection to the mathematical analogy: quality is not intrinsic to quantity, so the mathematician can consider quantity without quality; but by Thomas's own account infinity is intrinsic to deity.
claims: The analogy fails because infinity is intrinsic to deity while quality is not intrinsic to quantity.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e2073.summary: Reply: the analogy holds in the relevant respect, namely that the mode of being need not correspond uniformly to the mode of understanding; even if quality were intrinsic to quantity, the ratio of 'not-qualified' could belong to quantity extrinsically.
claims: Even what is intrinsic to a thing may be absent from it extrinsically in how it is considered.

HuYgTa-d1e933-d1e2090.summary: Final objection and reply: on this view the ratio of the object would seem extrinsic to the thing understood. Thomas answers that it is in one way intrinsic, since it is truly taken from the thing, and in another extrinsic, since it belongs to the thing according to a commensuration with something extrinsic, the intellect. Thus even the blessed understand the infinity intrinsic to deity, but finitely, given the required commensuration of object and power — just as the soul understands the undivided motion of heaven yet conceives it dividedly to complete the ratio of time. Such examples guide us toward the truth though they are not exact.
claims: The ratio of an object is intrinsic as taken from the thing and extrinsic as commensurated to the intellect.
The blessed understand divine infinity, but finitely.
Commensuration between object and power is necessarily required.

HuYgTa-d1e933.summary: Prologue, Question 1: whether God is subject of theology under the absolute, abyssal ratio of deity or under a special ratio. After setting out the general method of his questions (conclusion, contrary opinions refuted, confirmation, replies), Thomas concludes that God is subject under a special ratio — 'the supremely lovable truth proportioned to the rational soul not yet perfected by the light of glory' — named by reference to theology's end, the love of God. He refutes eight arguments of those who hold the absolute ratio, together with their attempts to avoid the consequence that theology would be infinite (by denying that infinity is of deity's formal ratio, by treating infinity as merely annexed, or by deriving a science's quantity from its receiving subject). He confirms his view by arguing that otherwise our science would be of the same species as God's and that theologians would know infinitely many things. He then aligns his view with Giles of Rome's 'Deus ut glorificator', defending that term against eight objections, and closes by explaining how a finite ratio can belong extrinsically to an intrinsically infinite object.
claims: God is the subject of our theology under a special, restricted ratio, not under the absolute, infinite ratio of deity.
Theology's subject is best named in relation to its end, the love of God and eternal glory.
Infinity belongs to the formal ratio of deity, so a theology considering deity under its absolute ratio would be infinite.
Our theology differs in species from God's own science and from the knowledge of the blessed.
The special ratio posits nothing intrinsic in God but belongs to him extrinsically as measure of a finite intellect.
Thomas's position agrees with Giles of Rome's account of God as glorifier.
